extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of mathematics; mathematicians interested in ancient Greek computational methods
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the notation, algorithms, and approximation strategies used by Greek mathematicians (Archimedes, Theon, Heron, Ptolemy) for arithmetic operations, extraction of square roots, and rational approximations to irrationals, including sexagesimal adaptations and historical generation methods (side- and diagonal-numbers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate powers/denominations in notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers were written so that the several powers of 10 (or 60 in the sexagesimal system) were kept separate, with hundreds, thousands, etc. written in separate vertical rows; the mental work corresponded to keeping denominations distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical representation of sums and subtractions places each power in its own column (hundreds, thousands, etc.). This permits carrying/borrowing and mental operations analogous to modern positional arithmetic. Example forms of addition and subtraction are given showing separate columns for powers of 10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexagesimal notation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In expressing sexagesimal quantities (degrees, minutes, seconds, or divisions of radius) Greeks used the ordinary numeral with one or more accents to indicate minutes, seconds, etc., and used a special sign (O) where a denomination had no units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: β΄ μ' for 47° 42’ 40"; Oa’ β΄ O’’ = 0° 1΄ 2" 0". Fractions for divisions of the radius were similarly denoted (τμήματα). Be explicit about accents and the symbol for zero when writing sexagesimal numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition and subtraction procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Addition and subtraction were carried out by keeping powers of the base separate and performing carries and borrows in the same conceptual manner as modern arithmetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write numbers in separate vertical rows by denomination and perform carries/borrows column-wise. The mental process matches our modern method; examples in the text illustrate typical written layouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication algorithm (Greek long multiplication)
rubrics_metrics.description: The multiplicand is written first, the multiplier below it preceded by ἐπί (‘into’). Multiply successively by the highest power of the multiplier down to the lowest; when fractions occur follow the same order with the fractional denominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceed by taking the highest power-of-ten term in the multiplier and multiplying it into each denomination of the multiplicand from highest to lowest; then continue with the next term in the multiplier. Examples from Eutocius and Heron demonstrate formation of partial products and summation to get the final product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division / long division procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Long division was performed by keeping denominations separate and estimating how many times the divisor fits into the highest grouped denominations; trial digits are chosen similarly to modern long division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate the leading quotient term by comparing high-denomination groups (e.g., 'how many times will 7 hundreds go into 60 myriads?'), multiply, subtract to get the remainder, and continue. The text contrasts a one-subtraction-per-quotient-term approach (more efficient) with Theon's method that sometimes makes multiple subtractions per term (longer and harder to predict successful trials). Sexagesimal long division adapts the same principles with minutes/seconds grouped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square root extraction (digit-by-digit method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extract the square root by partitioning the radicand into denominations, find the highest denomination term of the root (by trial as in long division), then use the identity (a + x)^2 = a^2 + 2a x + x^2 to choose successive digits x so that 2a x + x^2 is somewhat less than the current remainder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the root as a sum of denomination-terms (hundreds, tens, units, etc.). After subtracting a^2, divide the remainder by 2a (approximately) to suggest the next digit; choose the highest digit satisfying 2a x + x^2 ≤ remainder. Examples: square root of 144 found by taking 10 first, then 2 because 2·10·2 + 2^2 = 44.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexagesimal square-root extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the digit-by-digit square-root method in the sexagesimal system by treating fractional sexagesimal places as further denominations and using the Euclidean geometric basis for the procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express the remainder and subsequent calculations in sexagesimal fractions; choose successive sexagesimal digits (degrees, minutes, seconds) by testing the inequality analogous to 2a x + x^2 ≤ remainder. Theon’s exposition of extracting sqrt(4500 μοῖραι) illustrates the procedure and conversion between sexagesimal arithmetic and the (a+b)^2 identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedean inequality for bounding square roots
rubrics_metrics.description: When a^2 + b is not a square and a^2 is the nearest square, then the fractional part of sqrt(a^2 + b) satisfies b/(2a+1) < sqrt(a^2 + b) - a < b/(2a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this pair of inequalities to obtain rational bounds on the fractional part of a square root; it gives a simple way to choose an approximation slightly larger or smaller than the exact root. The text shows how Archimedes used such bounds to choose convenient rational approximations (upper and lower) to roots like sqrt(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting rational approximations for computational convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing rational approximations to irrationals for use in longer computations, prefer fractions that simplify later arithmetic (e.g., numerator 1, denominators powers of 2, or denominators that allow cancellation with later factors), and ensure the approximation is on the required side (not greater when a lower bound is needed, not less when an upper bound is needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Archimedes tends to take fractions with numerator 1 and denominators powers of 2 because they are easy to add and manipulate; he also selects approximations so that subsequent sums/divisions have convenient factors (e.g., choosing a fraction to make 5925 divisible by 13). He sometimes prefers a slightly less accurate but much more convenient approximation if it does not affect the final result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing approximations to facilitate later factor cancellation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick approximations that make later aggregate numerators/denominators divisible by desired factors to simplify subsequent steps (e.g., to enable division by 13 or 40), even if that leads to choosing a particular nearby rational approximation rather than the nearest one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete cases: in extracting a root whose fractional part will later be added to another number and divided by 780, choose the fractional approximation so that the resulting sum has factors simplifying division by 13; similarly, choose approximations that make sums divisible by 40 when that is convenient for subsequent work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Side-and-diagonal numbers method for approximating surds
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate sequences of integer pairs (side-numbers a_n and diagonal-numbers d_n) via the recurrence A_{n+1} = 2A_n + D_n, D_{n+1} = A_n + D_n (or the given recurrence in text) so that d_n^2 = 2 a_n^2 + 1 and the ratios d_n / a_n produce successive rational approximations to sqrt(2) (and analogous constructions for sqrt(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method (Theon of Smyrna’s side- and diagonal-numbers) yields a sequence of fractions approaching surds; the text shows how the sequence gives Pythagorean and later approximations, and how similar recurrences (and algebraic identities) can be used to generate approximations to sqrt(3) via solutions of x^2 - 3 y^2 = ±1 or related indeterminate equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracketing and iterative refinement for incommensurables
rubrics_metrics.description: Locate an irrational/surd between a greater and a lesser rational limit and then draw the limits closer by systematic application of algebraic identities or recurrence relations to obtain successively better rational bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Günther’s classification and the text’s exposition illustrate methods that bracket a value and iteratively refine bounds (one class of historical approaches). Zeuthen, Tannery, and others’ methods amount to producing sequences of closer upper and lower rational bounds, sometimes by solving related indeterminate equations.
